{{short description|Unoxidized tea}} {{about|a type of tea||Green Tea (disambiguation)}} {{Infobox beverage | name = Green tea | image = Green tea 3 appearances.jpg | caption = The appearance of green tea in three different stages (from left to right): the infused leaves, the dry leaves, and the liquid. | type = [[Tea]] | abv = | proof = | manufacturer = | distributor = | origin = [[China]] | introduced = | discontinued = | colour = Green | flavour = | ingredients = [[Camellia sinensis|Tea leaves]] | variants = | related = [[Tea]] | website = | region = [[East Asia]] }} {{infobox Chinese |t=綠茶 |s=绿茶 |kanji=緑茶 |hiragana=りょくちゃ |l=Green tea |fr=Thé vert |revhep=Ryoku-cha |kunrei=Ryoku-tya |p=lǜchá |w={{tone superscript|lü4-ch'a2}} |bpmf=ㄌㄩˋ ㄔㄚˊ |mi={{IPAc-cmn|l|ü|4|.|ch|a|2}} |j=luk6-caa4 |y=luhk-chàh |ci={{IPAc-yue|l|uk|6|.|c|aa|4}} |tl=li̍k-tê }} '''Green tea''' is a type of [[tea]] made from the [[leaves]] and [[bud]]s of the ''[[Camellia sinensis]]'' that have not undergone the [[Tea processing#General|withering and oxidation process]] that creates [[oolong tea]]s and [[black tea]]s.{{cite journal|vauthors=Khan N, Mukhtar H |title=Tea and health: studies in humans|journal=Current Pharmaceutical Design|volume=19|issue=34|pages=6141–7|date=2013|pmid= 23448443|pmc=4055352|type=Literature Review|doi=10.2174/1381612811319340008}} Green tea originated in [[China]] in the late 1st millennium BC, and since then its production and [[Manufacturing|manufacture]] has spread to other countries in East Asia. Several varieties of green tea exist, which differ substantially based on the variety of ''C. sinensis'' used, growing conditions, [[Horticulture|horticultural]] methods, production processing, and time of harvest. While it may slightly lower [[blood pressure]] and improve [[alertness]], current [[scientific evidence]] does not support most health benefit claims, and excessive intake of green tea [[extract]]s can cause [[liver damage]] and other [[side effect]]s. ==History== {{main|History of tea|History of tea in China}} [[File:Plantação de Chá Gorreana, Camellia sinensis, Ribeira Grande, ilha de São Miguel, Açores.JPG|thumb|The tea fields in the foothills of [[Gorreana]], [[Azores Islands]], Portugal: the only European region other than [[Agriculture in Georgia (country)|Georgia]] to support green tea production.]] Tea consumption has its legendary origins in China during the reign of mythological [[Emperor Shennong]].{{cite book |last1=Dattner |first1=Christine |last2=Boussabba |first2=Sophie |editor=Emmanuelle Javelle |title=The Book of Green Tea |year=2003|publisher=Universe Books|isbn=978-0-7893-0853-5|page=13}} A book written by [[Lu Yu]] in 618–907 AD, ''[[The Classic of Tea]]'' ({{lang-zh|t=[[wikt:茶|茶]][[wikt:經|經]]|s=|p=chájīng}}), is considered important in green tea history.{{citation needed|date=November 2024}} The ''Book of Tea'' (''Kissa Yōjōki'', lit. ''Record [of] Drinking Tea [for] [[Yangsheng (Daoism)|Nourishing Life]]''), written by [[Zen]] priest [[Eisai]] in 1211, describes how drinking green tea may affect five vital [[Organ (anatomy)|organs]], the shapes of tea plants, flowers and leaves, and how to grow and process tea leaves.{{citation needed|date=November 2024}} ==Steeping, brewing and serving== [[File:Four GreenTeas in White Bowls -1 (6196131680).jpg|alt=Four small white bowls of tea|thumb|Four varieties of green tea prior to brewing]] [[File:Green Tea Color.jpg|thumb|The colour of green tea brewed for 3 minutes at {{Convert|90|C}}]] [[Steeping]], or brewing, is the process of making tea from leaves and hot water, generally using {{Convert|2|g|2}} of tea per {{cvt|100|mL|}} of water or about {{tspUS|1}} of green tea per {{cvt|150|mL}} cup. Steeping temperatures range from {{Convert|61|C|}} to {{Convert|87|C|}} and steeping times from 30 seconds to three minutes. Generally, lower-quality green teas are steeped hotter and longer while higher-quality teas are steeped cooler and shorter, but usually multiple times (2–3 typically). Higher-quality teas like [[gyokuro]] use more tea leaves and are steeped multiple times for short durations. Steeping too hot or too long results in the release of excessive amounts of [[Tannins in tea|tannins]], leading to a bitter, [[astringent]] brew, regardless of initial quality. The brew's taste is also affected by the steeping technique; two important techniques are to warm the steeping container beforehand to prevent the tea from immediately cooling down, and to leave the tea leaves in the pot and gradually add more hot water during consumption.{{Citation needed|date=January 2018}} ==Production== In 2013, global production of green tea was approximately 1.7 million [[tonne]]s, with a forecast to double in volume by 2023.{{cite web|author1=Kaison, Chang|title=World tea production and trade: Current and future development|url=http://www.fao.org/3/a-i4480e.pdf|publisher=FAO Intergovernmental Group on Tea, Food and Agriculture Organization, United Nations|access-date=15 November 2017|location=Rome, Italy|date=2015}} As of 2015, China provided 80% of the world's green tea market, leading to its green tea exports rising by 9% annually, while exporting 325,000 tonnes in 2015.{{cite news|author1=Mingjie W|author2=Yue T|title=Why tea is Chinese to a tee|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/world/china-watch/business/chinese-tea-export-market/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170227203243/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/world/china-watch/business/chinese-tea-export-market/|archive-date=27 February 2017|access-date=15 November 2017|publisher=World News, The Telegraph|date=31 May 2016}} In 2015, the US was the largest importer of Chinese green tea (6,800 tonnes), an increase of 10% over 2014, and Britain imported 1,900 tonnes, 15% more than in 2014. ===Growing, harvesting and processing=== [[File:Processing green tea.jpg|thumb|Hand-rolling green tea after steaming]] Green tea is processed and grown in a variety of ways, depending on the type of green tea desired. As a result of these methods, maximum amounts of [[polyphenol]]s and [[volatile organic compounds]] are retained, affecting aroma and taste. The growing conditions can be broken down into two basic types − those grown in the sun and those grown under the shade. The green tea plants are grown in rows that are pruned to produce shoots in a regular manner, and in general are harvested three times per year. The first flush takes place in late April to early May. The second harvest usually takes place from June through July, and the third picking takes place in late July to early August. Sometimes, there will also be a fourth harvest. The first flush in the spring brings the best-quality leaves, with higher prices to match. Green tea is processed after picking using either artisanal or modern methods. Sun-drying, basket or charcoal firing, or pan-firing are common artisanal methods. Oven-drying, tumbling, or steaming are common modern methods.{{sfn|Heiss|Heiss|2007|pp=56–69}} Processed green teas, known as ''[[aracha]]'', are stored under low humidity refrigeration in 30- or 60-kilogram paper bags at {{convert|0|-|5|C|F}}. This aracha has yet to be refined at this stage, with a final firing taking place before [[Tea blending and additives|blending]], selection and packaging take place. The leaves in this state will be re-fired throughout the year as they are needed, giving the green teas a longer shelf-life and better flavour. The first flush tea of May will readily store in this fashion until the next year's harvest. After this re-drying process, each crude tea will be sifted and graded according to size. Finally, each lot will be blended according to the blending order by the tasters and packed for sale.{{citation|url=http://www.o-cha.com/green-tea-processing.htm|title=Green Tea Processing|publisher=O-cha.com|access-date=2013-01-13|archive-date=2013-01-18|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130118002747/http://www.o-cha.com/green-tea-processing.htm}} ===Import of radioactive Japanese tea=== On 17 June 2011, at [[Charles de Gaulle Airport|Charles de Gaulle airport]] in Paris, France, [[radioactive decay|radioactive]] [[caesium]] of 1,038 [[becquerel]]s per kilogram was measured in tea leaves imported from [[Shizuoka Prefecture]], Japan as a result of the [[Fukushima Daiichi nuclear disaster]] on 11 March, which was more than twice the restricted amount in the [[European Union]] of 500 becquerels per kilogram. The government of France announced that they rejected the leaves, which totalled {{convert|162|kg}}.[http://www.asahi.com/special/10005/TKY201106180245.html "日本からの緑茶に基準超えるセシウム パリの空港で検出."] (Japanese) ''[[Asahi Shimbun]]''. 2011-06-18. Retrieved 2011-06-19. In response, the governor of Shizuoka Prefecture, [[Heita Kawakatsu]], stated: "there is absolutely no problem when they [people] drink them because it will be diluted to about 10 becquerels per kilogram when they steep them even if the leaves have 1,000 becquerels per kilogram;" a statement backed by tests done in Shizuoka.[http://www.asahi.com/special/10005/TKY201106180410.html "静岡知事「飲用茶にすれば問題ない」 仏での検出受け."] (Japanese) ''Asahi Shimbun''. 2011-06-18. Retrieved 2011-06-19. Japanese Minister for Consumer Affairs and Food Safety [[Renhō]] stated on 3 June 2011 that "there are cases in which ''[[aracha]]'' {{bracket|whole leaves of Japanese green tea}} are sold as ''[[furikake]]'' {{bracket|condiments sprinkled on rice}} and so on and they are eaten as they are, therefore we think that it is important to inspect tea leaves including aracha from the viewpoint of consumers' safety."{{cite web |url= https://www.shizuokatea.com/blogs/green-tea-merchant/everything-you-need-to-know-about-aracha |title= Everything You Need To Know About Aracha |author= |date= October 4, 2022 |publisher= ShizuokaTea |access-date= April 25, 2026 |url-status=live |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20260425151722/https://www.shizuokatea.com/blogs/green-tea-merchant/everything-you-need-to-know-about-aracha |archive-date= April 25, 2026 }} In 2018, the US [[Food and Drug Administration]] updated its import status on Japanese products deemed to be contaminated by [[radionuclide]]s, indicating that tea from the [[Ibaraki prefecture]] had been removed from the list by the Government of Japan in 2015.{{cite web|title=Detention Without Physical Examination of Products from Japan Due to Radionuclide Contamination; Import Alert 99-33|url=https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/cms_ia/importalert_621.html|publisher=US Food and Drug Administration|access-date=13 April 2018|date=20 March 2018|archive-date=17 April 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180417192850/https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/cms_ia/importalert_621.html}} == Green tea across East Asia == [[File:Green Tea.jpg|thumb|right|A little cup of green tea]] === Mainland China and Taiwan === {{Infobox Chinese | title = Chinese name | pic = File:Longjing tea.jpg | piccap = ''[[Longjing tea|Longjing]]'', a green tea from [[Zhejiang]], China | t = {{lang|zh-Hant|綠茶}} | s = {{lang|zh-Hans|绿茶}} | p = lǜchá | showflag = p | w = lü4-ch'a2 | mi = {{IPAc-cmn|l|v|4|.|ch|a|2}} | psp = | myr = | gr = | bpmf = | mps = | xej = | zh-dungan = | sic = | j = luk6 caa4 | y = | gd = | hk = | mo = | ci = | toi = | gan = | wuu = | ngu = | hsn = | h = | poj = le̍k-tê | tl = | buc = | hhbuc = | mblmc = | lmz = | ouji = | suz = | teo = | hain = | lizu = }} {{Further|History of tea in China|Chinese tea|Chinese tea culture|Taiwanese tea|Taiwanese tea culture}} Loose leaf green tea has been the most popular form of tea in China since at least the [[Southern Song dynasty]].{{sfn|Mair|Hoh|2009|p=70}}{{sfn|Benn|2015|pp=7–8}} While Chinese green tea was originally steamed, as it still is in Japan, after the early [[Ming dynasty]] it has typically been processed by being pan-fired in a dry wok.{{sfn|Mair|Hoh|2009|pp=110–111}} Other processes employed in China today include oven-firing, basket-firing, tumble-drying and sun-drying.{{sfn|Heiss|Heiss|2007|pp=58–67}} Green tea is the most widely produced form of tea in China, with 1.42 million tons grown in 2014.{{cite web |script-title=zh:国家数据 |year=2014 |publisher=[[National Bureau of Statistics of China]] |url=http://data.stats.gov.cn/search.htm?s=绿毛茶产量(万吨)}} Popular green teas produced in China today include: * [[Biluochun|'''Green Snail Spring''']] ({{zhi|c=碧螺春|p=Bì luó chūn}})
Produced in [[Jiangsu]], this tea is named after the shape of the leaves, which are curled like snails.{{sfn|Heiss|Heiss|2007|p=124}} * [[Chun Mee|'''Precious Eyebrows''']] ({{zhi|c=珍眉|p=zhēn méi}})
Known in English by its Cantonese name, and popular outside China. It has a plum-like flavour.{{sfn|Chow|Kramer|1990|p=125}} *'''[[Gunpowder tea]]''' ({{zhi|c=珠茶|p=zhū chá}})
"Pearl tea", also called Gunpowder tea, is a form of tea which is tumble-dried so that each leaf is rolled into a small pellet that resembles [[gunpowder]].{{sfn|Heiss|Heiss|2007|p=65}} * [[Huangshan Maofeng|'''Yellow Mountain Fur Peak''']] ({{zhi|c=黄山毛峰|p=huángshān máofēng}})
A type of ''maofeng'' tea grown in the [[microclimate]] of the [[Huangshan]] mountain range in [[Anhui]] province. ''Maofeng'' teas are harvested by plucking intact two equal-sized leaves and a bud together.{{sfn|Heiss|Heiss|2007|pp=124–125}} * [[Longjing tea|'''Dragon Well''']] ({{zhi|c=龍井茶|p=lóngjǐng}})
Grown near [[Hangzhou]] in [[Zhejiang]] province, Longjing is the most well-known pan-fired Chinese green tea. Its flavour derives partly from the [[terroir]] of the region in which it is produced.{{sfn|Heiss|Heiss|2007|p=124}} * [[Lu'an Melon Seed tea|'''Lu'an Melon Seed''']] ({{zhi|c=六安瓜片|p=Lù'ān guāpiàn}})
Grown in [[Anhui]] province. Unlike typical Chinese teas, two leaves are plucked separately from each branch, with no bud and no stems. Harvested later in the season, it has a grassier flavour than typical Chinese green teas.{{sfn|Battle|2017|pp=106–107}} * [[Taiping houkui|'''Peaceful Monkey Leader''']] ({{zhi|c=太平猴魁|p=tàipíng hóukuí}})
Grown in [[Anhui]] province. Uses a [[cultivar]] with an unusually large leaf. The production process flattens the tea leaves, creating the so-called "two knives and a pole" shape from the leaves and stem.{{sfn|Battle|2017|pp=105-106}} * [[Maojian tea|'''Tippy Green''']] ({{zhi|c=信陽毛尖|p=Xìnyáng Máojiān}})
A type of ''maojian'' tea grown in [[Xinyang]], [[Henan]] province.{{sfn|Chow|Kramer|1990|p=143}} ''Maojian'' teas are harvested by plucking a bud and one leaf together.{{sfn|Heiss|Heiss|2007|pp=124–125}} * '''[[Anji bai cha|Anji White]]''' ({{zhi|c=安吉白|p=Ānjí bái}})
A type of green tea from Anji * '''[[Mengding Ganlu tea|Sweet Dew of Mengding]]''' ({{zhi|c=蒙頂甘露|p=Méngdǐng Gānlù}})
A yellowish-green tea with sweet aftertaste from Mending mountain in [[Sichuan]] * '''[[Duyun Maojian]]''' ({{zhi|c=都匀毛尖}})
One of the [[List of Chinese teas|famous Chinese teas]] which was a favourite of [[Mao Zedong]].Xie WeiBin, Xie WeiBin, Zhang GuoZhou Zhang GuoZhou, and Song LiSha Song LiSha. "Breeding of native tea varieties of Duyun Maojian." (2011): 33-38. * '''[[Cloud tea]]''' ({{zhi|c=雲雾茶|p=yún wù chá}})
A type of green tea originally cultivated in Le Mountain ({{zhi|c=南岳山|p=nányuè shān}}), named for the mountain clouds. It is mentioned in ''[[The Classic of Tea]]'' and is one of the [[List of Chinese teas|famous Chinese teas.]] === Japan === {{Further|History of tea in Japan}} {{see also|ja:日本茶}} [[File:2017 Kagoshima sencha.jpg|thumb|''[[Sencha]]'' green tea, the most popular form of tea in Japan]] Tea seeds were first brought to Japan in the early 9th century by the Buddhist monks [[Saicho]] and [[Kūkai]]. During the [[Heian period]] (794–1185), [[Emperor Saga]] introduced the practice of drinking tea to the imperial family. The [[Zen]] Buddhist priest [[Eisai]] (1141–1215), founder of the [[Rinzai school]] of Buddhism, brought tea seeds from China to plant in various places in Japan. Eisai advocated that all people, not just Buddhist monks and the elite, drink tea for its health benefits.{{sfn|Heiss|Heiss|2007|pp=164–166}} The oldest tea-producing region in Japan is [[Uji, Kyoto|Uji]], located near the former capital of [[Kyoto]].{{sfn|Heiss|Heiss|2007|pp=164–166}} It is thought that seeds sent by Eisai were planted in Uji, becoming the basis of the tea industry there.{{sfn|Mair|Hoh|2009|pp=85–86}} Today, Japan's most expensive premium teas are still grown in Uji.{{sfn|Heiss|Heiss|2007|pp=176–179}} The largest tea-producing area today is [[Shizuoka Prefecture]], which accounts for 40% of total Japanese [[sencha]] production.{{sfn|Battle|2017|p=156}}{{sfn|Heiss|Heiss|2007|pp=176–179}} Other major tea-producing regions include the island of [[Kyushu]] and the prefectures of [[Shiga Prefecture|Shiga]], [[Gifu Prefecture|Gifu]], and [[Saitama Prefecture|Saitama]] in central [[Honshu]].{{sfn|Heiss|Heiss|2007|pp=176–179}} [[File:AYATAKA, Green tea.jpg|thumb|right|A sample of bottled unsweetened [[iced tea|iced]] green tea produced by [[The Coca-Cola Company]] that is primarily sold in Japan under the brand name [[Ayataka]].]] All commercial tea produced in Japan today is green tea,{{sfn|Heiss|Heiss|2007|pp=169–170}} though for a brief period black tea was also produced in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Japanese tea production is heavily mechanized, and is characterized by the use of modern technology and processes to improve yields and reduce labour. Because of the high cost of labour in Japan, only the highest quality teas are plucked and processed by hand in the traditional fashion.{{sfn|Heiss|Heiss|2007|pp=167–168}} Japanese green teas have a thin, needle-like shape and a rich, dark green colour. Unlike Chinese teas, most Japanese teas are produced by steaming rather than pan-firing. This produces their characteristic colour, and creates a sweeter, more grassy flavour. A mechanical rolling/drying process then dries the tea leaves into their final shape.{{sfn|Heiss|Heiss|2007|pp=169–170}} The liquor of steamed Japanese tea tends to be cloudy due to the higher quantity of dissolved solids.{{sfn|Heiss|Heiss|2007|p=68}} Most Japanese teas are blended from leaves grown in different regions, with less emphasis on terroir than in the Chinese market. Because of the limited quantity of tea that can be produced in Japan, the majority of production is dedicated to the premium tea market. Cheaper bottled teas and tea-flavoured food products usually use lower-grade Japanese-style tea produced in China.{{sfn|Heiss|Heiss|2007|pp=174–175}} Although a variety of commercial tea cultivars exist in Japan, the vast majority of Japanese tea is produced using the ''Yabukita'' cultivar developed in the 1950s.{{sfn|Battle|2017|p=157}} Popular Japanese green teas include: * ''[[Bancha]]'' ({{lang|ja|番茶}})
A lower-grade tea plucked from the same bushes used to produce ''sencha''. It has a somewhat bolder flavour, and is plucked each season after ''sencha'' production is finished.{{sfn|Heiss|Heiss|2007|p=179}} * ''[[Genmaicha]]'' ({{lang|ja|玄米茶}})
Made by combining ''sencha'' tea leaves with toasted puffs of rice. * ''[[Gyokuro]]'' ({{lang|ja|玉露}})
Grown under shade for three weeks prior to plucking, ''gyokuro'' is one of the most exclusive varieties of tea produced in Japan.{{sfn|Battle|2017|p=162}} The shading technique imparts a sweeter flavour, and produces a particularly rich colour thanks to the higher amounts of [[chlorophyll]] in the shaded leaf. ''Gyokuro'' tea is associated with the Uji region, the first tea-growing region in Japan. It is often made using smaller-leaf cultivars of the tea plant.{{sfn|Heiss|Heiss|2007|pp=182–183}} * ''[[Hōjicha]]'' ({{lang|ja|焙じ茶}})
This type of tea is made by roasting ''sencha'' or ''bancha'' leaves with ''kukicha'' twigs.{{sfn|Heiss|Heiss|2007|p=185}} * ''[[Kabusecha]]'' ({{lang|ja|かぶせ茶}})
Similar to ''gyokuro'', kabusecha is shaded for only a week prior to plucking. Its flavour is somewhat between that of ''gyokuro'' and normal ''sencha''.{{sfn|Battle|2017|p=162}}{{sfn|Heiss|Heiss|2007|pp=182–183}} * ''[[Kukicha]]'' ({{lang|ja|茎茶}})
A blended tea made of ''sencha'' leaves and stems.{{sfn|Heiss|Heiss|2007|p=187}} * ''[[Matcha]]'' ({{lang|ja|抹茶}})
Like ''gyokuro'', ''matcha'' is shaded before plucking. The plucked and processed leaf is called ''tencha''. This product is then ground into a fine powder, which is ''matcha''. Because the tea powder is very perishable, ''matcha'' is usually sold in small quantities. It is typically rather expensive.{{sfn|Heiss|Heiss|2007|p=185}} ''Matcha'' is the type of tea used in the [[Japanese tea ceremony]]. It is prepared by whisking the tea with hot water in a bowl, until the surface is frothy. If the water is too hot, the tea may become overly bitter.{{sfn|Battle|2017|pp=163–164}} * ''[[Sencha]]'' ({{lang|ja|煎茶}})
This type of tea is produced throughout the tea season, and is the standard style today, representing 80% of all tea produced in Japan.{{sfn|Heiss|Heiss|2007|p=182}} 90% of ''sencha'' is grown from the ''Yabukita'' cultivar.{{sfn|Battle|2017|p=157}} * ''[[Shincha]]'' ({{lang|ja|新茶}})
The first early harvest of tea, plucked before the first flush, is called ''shincha''. ''Shincha'' is made from the youngest new growth leaves, and is plucked from early April to early May. ''Shincha'' typically refers to the early harvest of ''sencha'', but can refer to any type of tea plucked early in the season, before the main harvest. Because of the limited quantities in which it is produced, ''shincha'' is highly prized and expensive to obtain.{{sfn|Heiss|Heiss|2007|p=171}} === Korea === {{Further|Traditional Korean tea|Korean tea [[Bulgapsa]] (founded in 384, in [[Yeonggwang County|Yeonggwang]]), [[Bulhoesa]] (founded in 384, in [[Naju]]) and [[Hwaeomsa]] (founded in [[Gurye County|Gurye]], in 544) claim to be the birthplace of Korean tea culture. Green tea was commonly offered to Buddha, as well as to the spirits of deceased ancestors. Tea culture continued to prosper during the [[Goryeo]] period, with the tea offering being a part of the biggest national ceremonies and tea towns were formed around temples.{{Cite book|title=Cha saenghwal munhwa daejeon|last1=정|first1=동효|last2=윤|first2=백현|last3=이|first3=영희|publisher=Hong Ik Jae|year=2012|isbn=978-89-7143-351-5|location=Seoul|language=ko|script-title=ko:차생활문화대전|chapter=한국 전통차문화생활의 연대|chapter-url=http://terms.naver.com/entry.nhn?docId=1636514&cid=42752&categoryId=42754|via=[[Naver]]}} [[Zen|Seon]]-Buddhist manners of ceremony prevailed. During the [[Joseon]] period, however, Korean tea culture underwent secularization, along with the Korean culture itself. Korean ancestral rite ''[[jesa]]'', also referred to as ''[[charye]]'' ({{Korean|hangul=차례|hanja=茶禮|labels=no}}, "tea rite"), has its origin in ''[[darye]]'' ({{Korean|hangul=다례|hanja=茶禮|labels=no}}, "tea rite"), the practice of offering tea as simple ancestral rites by the [[House of Yi|royal family]] and the aristocracy in Joseon. Tea culture of Korea was actively suppressed by the Japanese during the [[Korea under Japanese rule|Japanese forced occupation]] period (1910‒1945), and the subsequent [[Korean War]] (1950‒1953) made it even harder for the Korean tea tradition to survive.{{cite book|last1=Brother Anthony of Taizé|author-link1=Brother Anthony|last2=Hong|first2=Kyeong-Hee|title=The Korean way of tea: an introductory guide|date=2007|publisher=Seoul Selection|location=Seoul|isbn=978-89-91913-17-2|pages=97–98}} The restoration of the Korean way of tea began in the 1970s, around [[Dasolsa]]. Commercial production of green tea in South Korea only began in the 1970s,.{{Cite journal|last=Lee|first=Geumdong|date=February 2014|script-title=ja:韓国における主要3茶産地形成期のリーダーの役割: 寶城郡, 河東郡, 済州道を事例に|trans-title=The Leaders' Contribution of the Formative Period of Korea's 3 Main Tea Producing Areas|url=http://portal.dl.saga-u.ac.jp/bitstream/123456789/121658/1/lee_201402.pdf|journal=佐賀大学農学部彙報|language=ja|volume=99|pages=1–20|access-date=2015-11-28|archive-date=2018-11-03|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181103020405/http://portal.dl.saga-u.ac.jp/bitstream/123456789/121658/1/lee_201402.pdf}} By 2012 the industry was producing 20% as much tea as Taiwan and 3.5% as much as Japan.{{cite web|url=http://faostat.fao.org/site/609/DesktopDefault.aspx?PageID=609|title=Crops Primary Equivalent|website=[[Food and Agriculture Organization Corporate Statistical Database|FAO Corporate Statistical Database]]|publisher=[[Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations]]|access-date=8 April 2017|archive-date=1 September 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160901005856/http://faostat.fao.org/site/609/DesktopDefault.aspx?PageID=609}}{{cite web|url=http://faostat.fao.org/site/567/DesktopDefault.aspx?PageID=567|title=Crops|website=[[Food and Agriculture Organization Corporate Statistical Database|FAO Corporate Statistical Database]]|publisher=[[Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations]]|access-date=8 April 2017|archive-date=19 June 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120619130038/http://faostat.fao.org/site/567/DesktopDefault.aspx?PageID=567}} Green tea is not as popular as coffee or other types of [[Traditional Korean tea|Korean tea]]s in modern South Korea. The annual consumption per capita of green tea in South Korea in 2016 was {{convert|0.16|kg|oz|frac=2|abbr=on}}, compared to {{convert|3.9|kg|lboz|abbr=on}} coffee.{{Cite news|url=http://www.segye.com/content/html/2016/07/24/20160724001339.html|script-title=ko:커피보단 쉼이 있는 '차문화' 부흥을|last=허|first=건량|date=23 July 2016|access-date=8 April 2017|language=ko|newspaper=[[Segye Ilbo]]}} Recently however, as the coffee market reached saturation point, South Korean tea production doubled during 2010‒2014,{{Cite news|url=http://www.sisaon.co.kr/news/articleView.html?idxno=48471|script-title=ko:"이제는 커피 대신 '차(茶)'다"...음료업계, 시장 선회|last=안|first=지예|date=12 October 2016|work=[[SisaON]]|access-date=8 April 2017|language=ko|issn=1976-9792}} as did tea imports during 2009–2015,{{Cite news|url=http://news.mk.co.kr/newsRead.php?no=716940&year=2016|script-title=ko:커피, 茶와의 동거...스타벅스 차 브랜드 '티바나' 10일만에 100만잔|last=이|first=새봄|date=2016-10-13|access-date=2017-02-19|language=ko|newspaper=[[Maeil Business Newspaper]]}} despite very high [[Tariff-rate quota|tariff rate]] (513.6% for green tea, compared to 40% for black tea, 8% for processed/roasted coffee, and 2% for raw [[coffee bean]]s). Korean green tea can be classified into various types based on several different factors. The most common is the flush, or the time of the year when the leaves are plucked (and thus also by leaf size). * ''[[Ujeon]]''
''Ujeon'' ({{Korean|hangul=우전|hanja=雨前|labels=no|links=no|lit="pre-rain"}}), or ''cheonmul-cha'' ({{Korean|hangul=첫물차|labels=no|links=no|lit="first flush tea"}}), is made of hand-picked leaves plucked before ''[[Guyu|gogu]]'' (20–21 April).{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vVudAAAAMAAJ|title=The Korean Way of Tea: An Introductory Guide|last1=Brother Anthony of Taizé|last2=Hong|first2=Kyeong-hee|publisher=Seoul Selection|year=2007|isbn=978-89-91913-17-2|location=Seoul|page=13|author-link=Brother Anthony}}{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tHCXDQAAQBAJ&pg=PT81|title=Modern Tea: A Fresh Look at an Ancient Beverage|last=Richardson|first=Lisa Boalt|publisher=Gilbut Publishing|year=2016|isbn=979-11-6050-037-0|location=Seoul|page=51|language=ko|translator-last=공|translator-first=민희|script-title=ko:차 상식사전|orig-date=2014}}{{Cite news|url=http://www.koreaherald.com/view.php?ud=20130614000762|title=Green as far as the eye can see|last=Jackson|first=Julie|date=14 June 2013|work=[[The Korea Herald]]|access-date=20 March 2017}} The ideal steeping temperature for ''ujeon'' tea is {{convert|50|C}}.{{Cite news|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KCAOAQAAMAAJ|title=Tradition - The Way of Tea: A Lifestyle Aesthetic for Learning the Depth and Enlightenment of Life|work=Pictorial Korea|publisher=[[Korean Overseas Culture and Information Service]]|year=2004|editor-last=Kim|editor-first=Young-mann|page=26|oclc=704162423}} * ''[[Sejak]]''
''Sejak'' ({{Korean|hangul=세작|hanja=細雀|labels=no|lit="thin sparrow"}}), or ''dumul-cha'' ({{Korean|hangul=두물차|labels=no|links=no|lit="second flush tea"}}), is made of hand-picked leaves plucked after ''[[Guyu|gogu]]'' (20–21 April) but before ''[[Lixia|ipha]]'' (5–6 May). The tea is also called ''[[jakseol]]'' ({{Korean|hangul=작설|hanja=雀舌|labels=no|links=no|lit="[[Passer montanus|sparrow]] tongue"}}) as the tea leaves are plucked when they are about the size of a [[Passer montanus|sparrow]]'s tongue. The ideal steeping temperature for ''sejak'' tea is {{convert|60-70|C}}. * ''[[Jungjak]]''
''Jungjak'' ({{Korean|hangul=중작|hanja=中雀|labels=no|links=no|lit="medium sparrow"}}), or ''semul-cha'' ({{Korean|hangul=세물차|labels=no|links=no|lit="third flush tea"}}), is made of leaves plucked after ''[[Lixia|ipha]]'' (5–6 May) until the mid May. The ideal steeping temperature for ''jungjak'' tea is {{convert|70-80|C}}. * ''[[Daejak]]''
''Daejak'' ({{Korean|hangul=대작|hanja=大雀|labels=no|links=no|lit="big sparrow"}}), or ''kkeunmul-cha'' ({{Korean|hangul=끝물차|labels=no|links=no|lit="final flush tea"}}), is made of tea leaves plucked in late May and after. It is usually made into [[tea bag]]s or used in cooking. The ideal steeping temperature for ''daejak'' tea is {{convert|80-90|C}}. The mode of preparation also differs: * ''[[Ipcha]]'' (''yeopcha'')
The synonyms ''ipcha'' ({{Korean|hangul=잎차|labels=no|links=no|lit="leaf tea"}}) and ''yeopcha'' ({{Korean|hangul=엽차|hanja=葉茶|labels=no|links=no|lit="leaf tea"}}) refer to loose leaf tea, often in contrast to tea in [[tea bag]]s. As the words mean "leaf tea", they can also be used in contrast to [[powdered tea]].{{Cite web|url=http://stdweb2.korean.go.kr/search/View.jsp?idx=241455|title=yeopcha|website=[[Standard Korean Language Dictionary]]|publisher=[[National Institute of Korean Language]]|script-title=ko:엽차|access-date=20 March 2017|archive-date=20 March 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170320144337/http://stdweb2.korean.go.kr/search/View.jsp?idx=241455}} * ''[[Garucha]]'' (''malcha'')
The synonyms ''garucha'' ({{Korean|hangul=가루차|labels=no|links=no|lit="powder tea"}}) and ''malcha'' ({{Korean|hangul=말차|hanja=末茶|labels=no|links=no|lit="powder tea"}}) refer to powdered tea.{{Cite web|url=http://stdweb2.korean.go.kr/search/View.jsp?idx=387082|title=garucha|website=[[Standard Korean Language Dictionary]]|publisher=[[National Institute of Korean Language]]|script-title=ko:가루차|access-date=20 March 2017|archive-date=20 March 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170320232633/http://stdweb2.korean.go.kr/search/View.jsp?idx=387082}}{{Cite web|url=http://stdweb2.korean.go.kr/search/View.jsp?idx=110967|title=malcha|website=[[Standard Korean Language Dictionary]]|publisher=[[National Institute of Korean Language]]|script-title=ko:말차|access-date=20 March 2017|archive-date=20 March 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170320232302/http://stdweb2.korean.go.kr/search/View.jsp?idx=110967}} Leaf teas are processed either by roasting or steaming. * ''[[Deokkeum-cha]]'' (''bucho-cha'')
Roasting is the most common and traditional way of tea processing in Korea. Also translated into "pan-fried tea", the ''deokkeum-cha'' ({{Korean|hangul=덖음차|labels=no|links=no|lit="roasted tea"}}) or ''bucho-cha'' ({{Korean|hangul=부초차|hanja=麩炒茶|labels=no|links=no|lit="roasted tea"}}) varieties are richer in flavour.{{Cite web|url=http://www.teachampionship.com/tc16/Public/Content.aspx?ID=1063020|title=2015 Spring Harvest Hot Tea Class Champions|website=Global Tea Championship|access-date=20 March 2017}}{{Cite book|script-title=ko:차생활문화대전|publisher=Hong Ik Jae|year=2012|isbn=978-89-7143-351-5|editor-last=정|editor-first=동효|location=Seoul|language=ko|chapter=deokkeum-cha|script-chapter=ko:덖음차|access-date=20 March 2017|editor-last2=윤|editor-first2=백현|editor-last3=이|editor-first3=영희|chapter-url=http://terms.naver.com/entry.nhn?docId=1634412|via=[[Naver]]}}{{Cite book|script-title=ko:차생활문화대전|publisher=Hong Ik Jae|year=2012|isbn=978-89-7143-351-5|editor-last=정|editor-first=동효|location=Seoul|language=ko|chapter=bucho-cha|script-chapter=ko:부초차|access-date=20 March 2017|editor-last2=윤|editor-first2=백현|editor-last3=이|editor-first3=영희|chapter-url=http://terms.naver.com/entry.nhn?docId=1634758|via=[[Naver]]}} * ''[[Jeungje-cha]]''
Steaming is less popular in Korean green tea processing, but the method is still used in [[Korean temple cuisine|temple cuisine]]. Tea prepared with steamed tea leaves, called ''jeungje-cha'' ({{Korean|hangul=증제차|hanja=蒸製茶|labels=no|links=no|lit="steamed tea"}}), are more vivid in colour.{{Cite book|script-title=ko:차생활문화대전|publisher=Hong Ik Jae|year=2012|isbn=978-89-7143-351-5|editor-last=정|editor-first=동효|location=Seoul|language=ko|chapter=jeungje-cha|script-chapter=ko:증제차|access-date=20 March 2017|editor-last2=윤|editor-first2=백현|editor-last3=이|editor-first3=영희|chapter-url=http://terms.naver.com/entry.nhn?docId=1635873|via=[[Naver]]}} Southern, warmer regions such as [[Boseong County|Boseong]] in [[South Jeolla Province]], [[Hadong County|Hadong]] in [[South Gyeongsang Province]], and [[Jeju Province|Jeju Island]] are famous for producing high-quality tea leaves.{{Cite web|url=http://english.visitkorea.or.kr/enu/FO/FO_EN_6_3_3_1.jsp|title=The World of Korean Tea – Nokcha (Green Tea)|website=[[Korea Tourism Organization]]|access-date=20 March 2017|archive-date=25 February 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170225222437/http://english.visitkorea.or.kr/enu/FO/FO_EN_6_3_3_1.jsp}} * ''[[Banya-cha]]''
''Banya-cha'' ({{Korean|hangul=반야차|hanja=般若茶|labels=no|links=no|lit="prajñā tea"}}) is one of the most renowned Korean green teas.{{Cite web|url=http://stdweb2.korean.go.kr/search/View.jsp?idx=426963|title=banya-cha|website=[[Standard Korean Language Dictionary]]|publisher=[[National Institute of Korean Language]]|script-title=ko:반야차|access-date=20 March 2017|archive-date=20 March 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170320144542/http://stdweb2.korean.go.kr/search/View.jsp?idx=426963}} This steamed tea is developed by Buddhist monks in [[Boseong County|Boseong]].{{Citation needed|date=March 2017}} The tea is grown on sandy loam near mountains and sea.{{Citation needed|date=March 2017}} The word ''banya'' is a Korean transliteration of the Buddhist concept ''[[Prajñā (Buddhism)|prajñā]]''. * ''[[Jungno-cha]]''
''Jungno-cha'' ({{Korean|hangul=죽로차|hanja=竹露茶|labels=no|links=no|lit="bamboo dew tea"}}) is one of the most renowned Korean green teas.{{Cite web|url=http://stdweb2.korean.go.kr/search/View.jsp?idx=484028|title=jungno-cha|website=[[Standard Korean Language Dictionary]]|publisher=[[National Institute of Korean Language]]|script-title=ko:죽로차|access-date=20 March 2017|archive-date=20 March 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170320144144/http://stdweb2.korean.go.kr/search/View.jsp?idx=484028}} The roasted variety of tea is made of tea leaves grown among the bamboo in [[Gimhae]], [[Hadong County|Hadong]], and [[Jinju]] in [[South Gyeongsang Province]].{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=GUhRLeac8AgC&pg=PA267|title=Ch'oŭi Ŭisun: A Liberal Sŏn Master and an Engaged Artist in Late Chosŏn Korea|last=Lee|first=Young Ho|publisher=Jain Publishing|year=2002|isbn=978-0-89581-950-5|location=Fremont, CA|page=267}} Green tea can be blended with other ingredients. * ''[[Hyeonmi-nokcha]]''
''Nokcha'' (green tea) blended with ''[[hyeonmi-cha]]'' (brown rice tea) is called ''hyeonmi-nokcha'' ({{Korean|hangul=현미녹차|hanja=玄米綠茶|labels=no|links=no|lit="brown rice green tea"}}). * ''[[Remon-nokcha]]''
''Nokcha'' (green tea) blended with lemon is called ''remon-nokcha'' ({{Korean|hangul=레몬 녹차|labels=no|links=no|lit="lemon green tea"}}). === Vietnam === [[file:Vietnamese green tea.jpg|thumb|Thái Nguyên green tea]] Green tea is the most popular tea among the [[Vietnamese people]]. In 2011, it accounted for over 63% of overall retail volume sales.{{cite web |title=Tea in Vietnam |url=http://marketpublishers.com/report/consumers_goods/food_beverage/tea_vietnam.html |access-date=29 November 2012 |publisher=Euromonitor International Ltd}} Vietnamese tea culture is ancient, but large scale cultivation was introduced in the late 19th century by [[French Indochina|French colonists]] who ran the first plantations in the [[Phú Thọ province|Phú Thọ area]]. Though less well known than Japanese and Chinese green teas, there are various types of Vietnamese green tea and various cultivars. They have recently entered the international market, usually at lower prices. Vietnam is fifth in the world for tea production today.{{Cite web |date=17 September 2020 |title=The World's Top Tea-Producing Countries |url=https://www.worldatlas.com/articles/the-worlds-top-10-tea-producing-nations.html |access-date=2022-09-06 |website=WorldAtlas |language=en-US}} There is a long tradition of growing and processing green tea in the [[Thái Nguyên]] area, north of Hanoi, which has been called the "cradle" of Vietnamese tea.{{cite web |title=Thai Nguyen - The Cradle of Vietnamese Tea |url=https://www.vietnamonline.com/destination/thai-nguyen/culture/cradle-vietnamese-tea.html |website=Vietnam Online}} This region is now known for its green tea, which is shipped internationally.{{cite news |date=20 June 2025 |title=Thai Nguyen Tea Conquers the World Market |url=https://www.vietnam.vn/en/che-thai-nguyen-chinh-phuc-thi-truong-the-gioi-ky-3-tang-cuong-xuat-khau-de-phat-trien-ben-vung |access-date=19 July 2025 |newspaper=Vietnam.vn}} There are also many scented varieties of Vietnamese green tea, most of which are scented with a certain flower petals. These include: * [[Vietnamese lotus tea|Lotus tea]] (''trà sen''), scented with [[Nelumbo nucifera|Lotus flowers]], sometimes the petals will be mixed into the tea leaves. * [[Jasmine#Cultivation and uses|Jasmine tea]] (''trà lài''), scented with [[jasmine]] * [[Chrysanthemum]] tea (''trà cúc'') * Aglaia tea (''trà ngâu'', tea infused with the flower from the [[Aglaia duperreana]] plant) * ''Trà sói'', tea infused with the flower from the [[Chloranthaceae]] family. * ''Trà sâm dứa'', made from a herbal mix of green tea, jasmine, [[Aglaia duperreana]] flower, basil and pandan leaves. ==Extracts== [[Polyphenol]]s found in green tea include [[epigallocatechin gallate]] (EGCG), [[epicatechin gallate]], [[epicatechin]]s and [[flavanol]]s, which are under laboratory research for their potential effects [[in vivo]]. Other components include three kinds of [[flavonoid]]s, known as [[kaempferol]], [[quercetin]], and [[myricetin]].Committee on Diet, Nutrition, and Cancer, Assembly of Life Sciences, National Research Council, Diet, nutrition, and cancer, Washington: D.C National Academies Press, 1982, p. 286. Although the mean content of [[flavonoid]]s and [[catechins]] in a cup of green tea is higher than that in the same volume of other food and drink items that are traditionally considered to promote health,USDA Database for the Flavonoid Content of Selected Foods, Release 2.1 (2007) flavonoids and catechins have no proven biological effect in humans.{{cite journal|author=EFSA Panel on Dietetic Products, Nutrition and Allergies |title=Scientific Opinion on the substantiation of health claims related to various food(s)/food constituent(s) and protection of cells from premature aging, antioxidant activity, antioxidant content and antioxidant properties, and protection of DNA, proteins and lipids from oxidative damage pursuant to Article 13(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1924/20061|journal= EFSA Journal|year= 2010|volume= 8|issue=2|page=1489|doi=10.2903/j.efsa.2010.1489|doi-access=free}} Green tea leaves are initially processed by soaking in an alcohol solution, which may be further concentrated to various levels; byproducts of the process are also packaged and used.{{citation needed|date=August 2021}} Extracts are sold over the counter in liquid, powder, capsule, and tablet forms,I.T. Johnson & G. Williamson, Phytochemical functional foods, Cambridge, UK: Woodhead Publishing, 2003, pp. 135–145A. Bascom, Incorporating herbal medicine into clinical practice, Philadelphia: F.A. Davis Company, 2002, p. 153. and may contain up to 17.4% of their total weight in caffeine,{{Cite journal|last1=Seeram|first1=Navindra P.|last2=Henning|first2=Susanne M.|last3=Niu|first3=Yantao|last4=Lee|first4=Rupo|last5=Scheuller|first5=H. Samuel|last6=Heber|first6=David|date=2006-03-01|title=Catechin and Caffeine Content of Green Tea Dietary Supplements and Correlation with Antioxidant Capacity|journal=Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry|volume=54|issue=5|pages=1599–1603|doi=10.1021/jf052857r|pmid=16506807|bibcode=2006JAFC...54.1599S |issn=0021-8561}} though decaffeinated versions are also available.{{cite web|title=Update on the USP Green Tea Extract Monograph|url=http://www.usp.org/usp-nf/notices/retired-compendial-notices/update-usp-green-tea-extract-monograph|publisher=USP|language=en|date=April 10, 2009}} Green tea extract is usable as a [[clean label]] [[food preservative]], protecting fats from rancidity. The oil-soluble form used is palmitoylated green tea catechins, ruled [[generally recognized as safe]] in 2020.{{cite web |title=FDA has no objections to GRAS status of Kemin's oil-soluble green tea extract GT-FORT |url=https://www.foodnavigator-usa.com/Article/2019/02/22/FDA-has-no-objections-to-GRAS-status-of-Kemin-s-oil-soluble-green-tea-extract-GT-FORT |website=foodnavigator-usa.com|date=22 February 2019 }} [https://web.archive.org/web/20211123081902/https://www.fda.gov/files/food/published/GRAS-Notice-GRN-772-Agency-Response-Letter.pdf Re: GRAS Notice No. GRN 000772, from FDA] ==Health effects == {{Main|Health effects of tea}} {{Infobox nutritional value | name = Brewed, regular green tea | kJ = 4 | carbs = 0 g | fat = 0 g | protein = 0.2 g | calcium_mg = 0 | magnesium_mg = 1 | manganese_mg = 0.18 | iron_mg = 0.02 | potassium_mg = 8 | sodium_mg = 1 | thiamin_mg = 0.007 | riboflavin_mg = 0.06 | niacin_mg = 0.03 | vitB6_mg = 0.005 | vitC_mg = 0.3 | opt1n = Water | opt1v = 99.9 g | opt2n = Caffeine | opt2v = 12 mg | note = [https://web.archive.org/web/20170707194019/https://ndb.nal.usda.gov/ndb/foods/show/4329?fgcd=&man=&lfacet=&count=&max=&sort=&qlookup=&offset=&format=Full&new=&measureby= Link to Full USDA Nutrient Report] }} Regular green tea is 99.9% water, provides 1 kcal per 100 mL serving, is devoid of significant [[nutrient]] content (table), and contains [[phytochemical]]s an active anti-inflammatory and antioxidant such as [[polyphenol]]s and [[caffeine]]. Numerous claims have been made for the health benefits of green tea, but human [[clinical research]] has not found good evidence of benefit.{{cite web |date=September 2016 |title=Green tea |url=https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/greentea |access-date=12 August 2018 |publisher=National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, US National Institutes of Health |quote=Green tea extracts haven't been shown to produce a meaningful weight loss in overweight or obese adults. They also haven't been shown to help people maintain a weight loss.}}{{cite web|url=http://www.efsa.europa.eu/en/efsajournal/pub/2055|publisher=European Food Safety Authority|title=Scientific Opinion on the substantiation of health claims related to Camellia sinensis (L.) Kuntze (tea), including catechins in green tea, and improvement of endothelium-dependent vasodilation (ID 1106, 1310), maintenance of normal blood pressure (ID 1310, 2657), maintenance of normal blood glucose concentrations (ID 1108), maintenance of normal blood LDL cholesterol concentrations (ID 2640), protection of the skin from UV-induced (including photo-oxidative) damage (ID 1110, 1119), protection of DNA from oxidative damage (ID 1120, 1121), protection of lipids from oxidative damage (ID 1275), contribution to normal cognitive function (ID 1117, 2812), "cardiovascular system" (ID 2814), "invigoration of the body" (ID 1274, 3280), decreasing potentially pathogenic gastro-intestinal microorganisms (ID 1118), "immune health" (ID 1273) and "mouth" (ID 2813) pursuant to Article 13(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006|date=8 April 2011|doi=10.2903/j.efsa.2011.2055 |access-date=9 November 2014}}{{cite journal |last1=Filippini |first1=T |last2=Malavolti |first2=M |last3=Borrelli |first3=F |last4=Izzo |first4=AA |last5=Fairweather-Tait |first5=SJ |last6=Horneber |first6=M |last7=Vinceti |first7=M |title=Green tea (Camellia sinensis) for the prevention of cancer. |journal=Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews |date=March 2020 |volume=3 |issue=11 |article-number=CD005004 |doi=10.1002/14651858.CD005004.pub3 |pmid=32118296 |pmc=7059963 }} In 2011, a panel of scientists published a report on the claims for health effects at the request of the [[European Commission]]: in general they found that the claims made for green tea were not supported by sufficient scientific evidence. Although green tea may enhance [[alertness|mental alertness]] due to its [[caffeine]] content, there is only weak, inconclusive evidence that regular consumption of green tea affects the risk of [[cancer]] or [[cardiovascular diseases]], and there is no evidence that it benefits [[weight loss]]. In some cases of excessive consumption, green tea extract is [[hepatotoxic]] with evidence of liver damage.{{cite journal |vauthors=Brown AC |title=Liver toxicity related to herbs and dietary supplements: Online table of case reports. extract:
Green tea is a type of tea made from the leaves and buds of the Camellia sinensis that have not undergone the withering and oxidation process that creates oolong teas and black teas. Green tea originated in China in the late 1st millennium BC, and since then its production and manufacture has spread to other countries in East Asia.
Several varieties of green tea exist, which differ substantially based on the variety of C. sinensis used, growing conditions, horticultural methods, production processing, and time of harvest. While it may slightly lower blood pressure and improve alertness, current scientific evidence does not support most health benefit claims, and excessive intake of green tea extracts can cause liver damage and other side effects.
